== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Moderate concern / Unclear: 554 itineraries (including 92 residential itineraries) were dropped at the outset due to missing geographical coordinates; reservoir water production metering was only available from November 2016 to May 2018 due to meter breakages; rationing schedules were restricted to October 2016-December 2018; and the completeness of monthly customer meter readings across the 132 months (2008-2018) per itinerary is not reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: The multivariable negative binomial mixed-effects model adjusts for only three ecological covariates (residential zoning category, built-up settlement age, and modelled itinerary population, plus a random effect for year) due to unavailable small-area census statistics. Unmeasured household socio-economic heterogeneity, commercial/productive water use within residential connections, private water storage capacity, and off-grid water sources create substantial residual confounding and ecological fallacy risk.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate: Official administrative residential zoning classifications (R1-R4 derived from the 1973 Master Plan / 1985 water distribution plans and updated via the 2014 Nairobi Integrated Urban Development Master Plan), NCWSC domestic block tariffs (2015-2018), and formal weekly rationing schedules (2016-2018) are sourced directly from utility and ministry records and cross-validated against KSCBS tenure/slum indicators, though informal land-use transitions, an unexplained sharp 2013 reclassification shift, and unenforced private kiosk retail pricing introduce administrative proxy error.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: Outcome per-capita domestic consumption divides NCWSC billed meter volumes by WorldPop random-forest modelled grid populations, omitting 29% non-revenue water (including illegal connections, leaks, and irregular/unmetered connections), omitting alternative water sources (vendors, boreholes, tankers), and conflating residential economic/commercial water use with domestic consumption. Exposure zoning categories rely on coarse built-environment/land-use proxies with an abrupt 2013 population shift between R1 and R4.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (high risk of measurement error): While water sufficiency uses Gleick's standard >1500 L/capita/month benchmark, numerator data come solely from billed utility customer meters (missing unbilled/illegal consumption within the 29% non-revenue water loss and all non-piped water sources, while including small-scale commercial uses) and denominator data rely on dasymetric gridded population projections that include unpiped residents within itinerary boundaries and mask intra-itinerary household inequality.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-registered protocol or pre-analysis plan is reported, and multivariable covariate selection relied on univariable p < 0.2 screening. Several internal numerical inconsistencies appear in the published text and tables, including mismatched itinerary filtering counts/percentages (PDF Page 5), a reversed inequality sign for 2018 R4 density in Table 2 (<18,000), low-income built-up subgroup counts summing to 263 versus 252 total in Table 4, and an incompatible p-value (0.425) for a rate ratio of 0.54 (95% CI: 0.53-0.56) in Table 4.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: The study frame is restricted to NCWSC piped water billing itineraries, systematically excluding informal and newly settled residential neighbourhoods outside the municipal piped network, and additionally excludes 554 itineraries (including 92 residential itineraries) lacking geographical coordinates without comparing included versus excluded areas.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Inclusion criteria for the analytical sample are clearly stated: NCWSC water billing itineraries in Nairobi County for 2008-2018 that were classified as residential and possessed valid geographical coordinates (n = 2,380 residential itineraries retained after filtering out non-geolocated and non-residential itineraries), supplemented by 1,137 Nairobi household respondents across seven sublocations from the 2012-2013 KSCBS for classification validation (note minor arithmetic discrepancies in the authors' raw filtering totals on PDF Page 5).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: The setting and spatial units are thoroughly described, covering Nairobi County's demographics, water sources (Kikuyu Springs and Ruiru, Sasumua, and Thika dams), treatment and reservoir infrastructure (Gigiri and Kabete), tariff blocks, rationing schedules, itinerary size (~700 residents), and the four residential categories (R1-R4) across 1985 and 2018.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 3-6, Sections 2.1, 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.1.3, and 3.1; Tables 1-2; Figures 1-2

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Exposures combine administrative residential zoning maps (NCWSC / Ministry of Lands R1-R4), Landsat-derived GHS-Built settlement age (30x30m grid), and WorldPop random-forest gridded population estimates (100x100m grid). Although cross-tabulation against KSCBS household data supports R1-R4 as a broad proxy for socio-economic status, the authors acknowledge that built-environment classifications omit actual household socio-economic conditions, WorldPop small-area projections carry modelling uncertainty at itinerary scale, and Figure 3 exhibits an unexplained abrupt single-year shift in 2013 (-42% in R1 and +37% in R4 population).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-6 and 9-11, Sections 2.1.2, 2.2, 2.3, 3.1, 3.3.1, and 4; Figure 3; Supplemental Table 1A

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Water sufficiency was defined using Gleick's (1996) established international domestic benchmark (>1500 L per capita per month, equivalent to 50 L/capita/day), residential zoning followed official Nairobi planning instruments (1973 Master Plan / 2014 Integrated Urban Development Master Plan), and KSCBS socio-economic validation applied standard UN-Habitat slum household indicators.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-5 and 8, Sections 2.1.2, 2.3, and Figure 5 caption

domain_ratings.justification: The authors identified itinerary population size, neighbourhood built-up age, seasonal/annual hydrological variation, and residential-by-age interactions, and explicitly identified unmeasured confounders in the Discussion (commercial/economic water use within residential connections, household water storage capacity, shared connection types, alternative non-piped water sources, and missing census small-area socio-economic covariates).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Although a multivariable negative binomial mixed-effects model adjusted for residential category, built-up era, their interaction, itinerary population, and year random effects, the authors state they were restricted to only three covariates due to unavailable census small-area data. No analytical strategy addressed intra-itinerary ecological confounding, commercial water use on residential meters, unpiped residents within itinerary boundaries, or alternative water supply sources.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5-6 and 11, Sections 2.3 and 4; Table 4

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Monthly per-capita domestic water consumption was estimated by dividing aggregated NCWSC customer billing meter readings by WorldPop modelled itinerary populations. This measure omits 29% non-revenue water (including illegal connections and irregular/unmetered consumption, which disproportionately affect informal/low-income areas), omits non-utility water sources (kiosks/vendors/boreholes), conflates residential commercial activities with domestic consumption, and relies on modelled population denominators rather than actual metered household users.

While negative binomial mixed-effects modelling with VIF collinearity checks and residual diagnostics is broadly suitable for overdispersed count/rate data, the model specifies only year as a random effect without accounting for itinerary-level repeated-measures clustering or spatial autocorrelation (despite reporting a spatial autocorrelation test p-value of 0.028 on PDF Page 9), and Table 4 contains internal statistical contradictions (e.g., Built up before 1975 rate ratio 0.54 with 95% CI 0.53-0.56 reported alongside p = 0.425, and subgroup counts summing to 263 rather than 252).
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 5-6, 9, and 10, Sections 2.3 and 3.3.1; Table 4

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: High concern overall under the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies (no numeric score computed). Mutono et al. (2022) assemble an informative 11-year spatially disaggregated utility billing dataset across 2,380 residential itineraries in Nairobi (2008-2018), clearly describe Nairobi's water supply and tariff/rationing architecture, apply an objective domestic sufficiency threshold (>1500 L/capita/month), and cross-validate utility residential land-use classes against 1,137 households in the 2012-2013 KSCBS. However, substantial methodological risks limit internal validity: (1) selection bias from excluding off-grid informal settlements altogether and dropping 554 itineraries (92 residential) lacking geolocation; (2) outcome measurement bias from dividing NCWSC billed meter volumes (which miss 29% non-revenue water including illegal/irregular meters, omit off-grid/vended water sources, and include non-domestic commercial uses) by modelled WorldPop grid populations; (3) ecological fallacy and unmeasured confounding in a multivariable model restricted to three ecological covariates; and (4) unaddressed spatial residual autocorrelation (p = 0.028) and internal numerical/statistical inconsistencies in Table 4 and sample filtering counts.
raw_response.study_design_identified: Retrospective spatio-temporal ecological observational study (administrative utility billing panel and geospatial mixed-effects regression across 2,380 residential itineraries, 2008-2018, with cross-sectional household survey validation)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Methods and data sources on PDF Pages 3-6 (Sections 2.1-2.3); descriptive, rationing, and regression results on PDF Pages 6-10 (Sections 3.1-3.3.1, Tables 1-4, Supplemental Table 1A, Figures 1-6); methodological limitations on PDF Page 11 (Section 4 Discussion).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is an observational ecological regression examining differences in billed per-capita domestic water consumption across administrative residential zoning categories (R1-R4) and settlement built-up eras without any policy/intervention comparator or quasi-experimental evaluation structure (ruling out ROBINS-I) and without following outcome-free cohorts for incident outcomes (ruling out JBI Cohort Studies). Although monthly meter readings span 2008-2018, the primary exposures (residential zoning class and GHS built-up period) are static spatial classifications analyzed via a negative binomial regression with year as a random intercept and validated cross-sectionally against KSCBS household data, making the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies the closest-fitting instrument.
